counterexample: Take n = 2 with L_1 x = x' = 0 and L_2 x = x' = 1 (i.e. f_1 = 0, f_2 = 1). The proposed reduction to a two-equation system is exactly the case the induction never establishes, and the only available combining move (adding the equations) gives 2x' = 1, which is satisfied by x = t/2 while the original conjunction is unsatisfiable; so no psi-free-of-x conjunct can repair the equivalence.
reasoning_summary: Steps 0001-0003 are fine: applying the (strong) inductive hypothesis to the first k equations legitimately yields Lx = f AND psi with psi free of x. Step 0004 is where the argument fails. It forms a new system phi' consisting of the newly produced equation Lx = f together with the leftover (k+1)-st equation, and asserts 'the size of new phi is less than k so you are fine'. (a) The assertion is literally false for small k: phi' has size 2, which is not less than k when k <= 2. (b) More fundamentally, the appeal is circular: the whole induction is anchored only at the base case n = 1, so strong induction can license the 2-equation case only if the 2-equation case has itself been proved, and it never is. Reducing n = k+1 to n = 2 therefore does not close the induction; it just relocates the unsolved crux, namely how to merge two equations in x into a single one. That crux is genuinely false as the original post attempts it, since replacing L_1 x = f_1 AND L_2 x = f_2 by (L_1+L_2)x = f_1+f_2 is only an implication, not an equivalence (e.g. x' = 0 AND x' = 1 is unsatisfiable while 2x' = 1 is satisfiable). The 'alternatively, split into halves' remark in step 0006 has exactly the same defect: both halves reduce to one equation each, leaving the same unproved 2-equation merge. Stopping at step 0004.
